title: Nilakantha Moves the Planets Around the Sun

title_i18n.en: Nilakantha Moves the Planets Around the Sun

subtitle: When the Sky Became a Calculated Circle
region: Trikkandiyur, Kelallur Illam and Kerala's scholarly network
moral: Innovation can revise a tradition from within.

sources.note: Precisely dated Sanskrit synthesis of planetary theory, spherical astronomy and series results.

sources.citation: Nilakantha Somayaji, Aryabhatiya-bhasya and Jyotirmimamsa, ed. K.V. Sarma
sources.note: Primary sources for his revised planetary model and observational method.

sources.citation: Ramasubramanian, Srinivas and Sriram, Current Science 66:9 (1994); K.V. Sarma and K. Ramasubramanian, Tantrasangraha translation (2011)
sources.note: Modern interpretation of the geo-heliocentric model and full translation of the text.

panels.shot: epic low-angle wide of Nilakantha on a temple rooftop under a star-filled Kerala sky

dialogue.text: In fifteenth-century Kerala, Nilakantha Somayaji watched the planets with a scholar’s eye, and quietly moved them around the Sun without moving the Earth.

panels.shot: quiet interior mid-shot, low-angle from floor looking up at a young boy

dialogue.text: Born in 1444 at Kelallur Illam near Trikkandiyur, Nilakantha grew up in a house where the sky was recited, measured and revered.

panels.shot: top-down close-up on hands and manuscripts

dialogue.text: He read Aryabhatiya and the classic siddhantas, absorbing a cosmos with Earth at the centre, planets bound by circles and epicycles.

panels.shot: wide evening shot of courtyard observatory, gentle three-quarter angle

dialogue.text: But Kerala’s scholars did not only recite. They measured. With shadows and sight-lines, they checked the old numbers against the living sky.

panels.shot: medium close-up profile as he peers through a simple sighting device

dialogue.text: Night after night, Nilakantha tracked Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, counting degrees, testing tables, feeling small mismatches prickle in his mind.

panels.shot: interior medium shot, candlelit debate with unseen elders implied off-frame

dialogue.speaker: nilakantha_somayaji
dialogue.text: Revered sirs, the sky strays from these numbers. Should we not ask why?

panels.shot: slow push-in on contemplative face, background of hanging palm-leaf bundles

dialogue.text: He chose a demanding path: to comment on Aryabhatiya, to write Jyotirmimamsa, and to test inherited astronomy verse by verse against observation.

panels.shot: wide shot of Kerala landscape under starry sky, Nilakantha small in foreground

dialogue.text: Aryabhata’s geocentric world remained sacred. The Earth stayed fixed. But for the wandering planets, Nilakantha allowed his geometry to wander further than tradition.

panels.shot: diagrammatic over-the-shoulder shot of his drawn orbit scheme on palm leaf

dialogue.text: He imagined a Sun that circled Earth, yet carried Mercury and Venus with it, and placed Mars, Jupiter and Saturn in paths tied to the Sun’s own journey.

panels.shot: tight close-up on his hand drawing careful arcs and annotating angles

dialogue.text: Planet by planet, he refined their equations, making computed longitudes match the observed sky more closely than older siddhantas could.

panels.shot: interior wide shot of writing desk piled with manuscripts, night turning to dawn

dialogue.text: Around 1500, he wove his work into Tantrasangraha—four hundred and thirty-two verses of planetary theory, spherical astronomy and subtle series calculations.

panels.shot: medium shot of him inscribing a chronogram verse, slight low angle

dialogue.text: He marked his time with chronograms and reckoned Kali days, anchoring his achievement to specific years instead of leaving it to vague tradition.

panels.shot: scholarly gathering wide shot in a temple hall, seated circle

dialogue.speaker: nilakantha_somayaji
dialogue.text: The Earth stands still, as taught. Yet the Sun can bear the planets and still honour our scriptures.

panels.shot: close-up on two scholars’ faces, one skeptical, one thoughtful, Nilakantha blurred behind

dialogue.text: His model did not assault geocentric cosmology. It revised it from within, balancing reverence and innovation so his new orbits could be heard.

panels.shot: montage-style wide shot: overlay of sky and geometric diagram

dialogue.text: Modern readers see in his geometry a pattern later echoed in Tycho’s model: planets circling the Sun, the Sun circling a central Earth.

panels.shot: medium shot of aged Nilakantha writing Siddhanta-darpana, serene front angle

dialogue.text: In Siddhanta-darpana he recorded his own date—Kali-day 1,660,181—fixing his life between 1444 and the years that followed, an unusual precision in Indian scholarly memory.

panels.shot: wide shot of Kerala coastline with temples, Nilakantha ghostlike figure in sky

dialogue.text: Around him, Kerala’s network of mathematicians continued to refine series and astronomy, building quietly on the foundations he had set down.

panels.shot: interior close-up of a modern scholar’s hands opening Tantrasangraha manuscript, Nilakantha’s portrait in background

dialogue.text: Centuries later, editors and historians like K.V. Sarma and Ramasubramanian traced his verses, rediscovered his planetary scheme and measured its closeness to later European models.

panels.shot: final epic wide shot of star-filled sky above Kerala, camera looking straight up

dialogue.text: Nilakantha Somayaji’s legacy endures as a lesson that even within a cherished tradition, a patient mind can redraw the heavens and make them fit the world more truly.
